\section{Declarations}

\begin{definition}[Finite decision trees]
\lean{FABL.FiniteDecisionTree}
\statementsource{Analysis-of-Boolean-Functions-by-Ryan-ODonnell}{
  pdf-ffbe9c7b3306-p073-b004,
  pdf-ffbe9c7b3306-p087-b004,
  pdf-ffbe9c7b3306-p094-b006,
  pdf-ffbe9c7b3306-p230-b001
}
\label{FABL.FiniteDecisionTree}
\leanok
For an alphabet $\Omega$, a set of labels $\alpha$, a natural number $n$, and an
available set $A\subseteq\{0,\ldots,n-1\}$ of coordinates, a finite decision tree is
either a leaf carrying a label in $\alpha$, or a query at a coordinate in $A$ with one
child tree for each possible answer in $\Omega$. Each child has the available set with
the queried coordinate removed.
\end{definition}

\begin{definition}[Full finite alphabet decision tree]
\lean{FABL.FiniteAlphabetDecisionTree}
\statementsource{Analysis-of-Boolean-Functions-by-Ryan-ODonnell}{
  pdf-ffbe9c7b3306-p073-b004,
  pdf-ffbe9c7b3306-p230-b006
}
\label{FABL.FiniteAlphabetDecisionTree}
\leanok
\uses{FABL.FiniteDecisionTree}
For an alphabet $\Omega$, a set of labels $\alpha$, and a natural number $n$, a full
finite alphabet decision tree is a finite decision tree whose initially available set
consists of all coordinates $\{0,\ldots,n-1\}$.
\end{definition}

\begin{definition}[Decision tree evaluation]
\lean{FABL.FiniteDecisionTree.eval}
\statementsource{Analysis-of-Boolean-Functions-by-Ryan-ODonnell}{
  pdf-ffbe9c7b3306-p073-b004,
  pdf-ffbe9c7b3306-p087-b004,
  pdf-ffbe9c7b3306-p094-b006,
  pdf-ffbe9c7b3306-p230-b001
}
\label{FABL.FiniteDecisionTree.eval}
\leanok
\uses{FABL.FiniteDecisionTree}
Let $T$ be a finite decision tree with alphabet $\Omega$ and labels $\alpha$, and let
$x\in\Omega^n$ be an input. Its evaluation returns the label at a leaf; at a query of
coordinate $i$, it follows the child indexed by $x_i$ and evaluates that child on the
same input.
\end{definition}

\begin{definition}[Decision tree query trace]
\lean{FABL.FiniteDecisionTree.queryTrace}
\label{FABL.FiniteDecisionTree.queryTrace}
\leanok
\uses{FABL.FiniteDecisionTree}
Let $T$ be a finite decision tree whose queries use coordinates from a finite set, and
let $x$ assign an alphabet symbol to each coordinate. The query trace of $T$ on $x$ is
the ordered list of coordinates queried along the path determined by $x$; it is empty at
a leaf.
\end{definition}

\begin{definition}[Decision tree query set]
\lean{FABL.FiniteDecisionTree.querySet}
\label{FABL.FiniteDecisionTree.querySet}
\leanok
\uses{FABL.FiniteDecisionTree, FABL.FiniteDecisionTree.queryTrace}
Let $T$ be a finite decision tree over the coordinate set $\mathrm{Fin}(n)$ and alphabet
$Ω$, and let $x$ assign an alphabet symbol to each coordinate. The query set of $T$ on
$x$ is the set of coordinates appearing in its query trace.
\end{definition}

\begin{definition}[Decision tree query count]
\lean{FABL.FiniteDecisionTree.queryCount}
\label{FABL.FiniteDecisionTree.queryCount}
\leanok
\uses{FABL.FiniteDecisionTree, FABL.FiniteDecisionTree.queryTrace}
Let $T$ be a finite decision tree over the coordinate set $\mathrm{Fin}(n)$ and alphabet
$Ω$, and let $x$ assign an alphabet symbol to each coordinate. The query count of $T$ on
$x$ is the length of its query trace.
\end{definition}

\begin{definition}[Decision tree leaf count]
\lean{FABL.FiniteDecisionTree.leafCount}
\statementsource{Analysis-of-Boolean-Functions-by-Ryan-ODonnell}{pdf-ffbe9c7b3306-p074-b002}
\label{FABL.FiniteDecisionTree.leafCount}
\leanok
\uses{FABL.FiniteDecisionTree}
Let $\Omega$ be finite, and let $T$ be a finite decision tree with alphabet $\Omega$ and
labels $\alpha$. Its leaf count is $1$ for a leaf; at a query, it is the sum of the leaf
counts of the child trees over all answers in $\Omega$.
\end{definition}

\begin{definition}[Decision tree depth]
\lean{FABL.FiniteDecisionTree.depth}
\statementsource{Analysis-of-Boolean-Functions-by-Ryan-ODonnell}{
  pdf-ffbe9c7b3306-p074-b002,
  pdf-ffbe9c7b3306-p087-b004,
  pdf-ffbe9c7b3306-p094-b006,
  pdf-ffbe9c7b3306-p230-b001
}
\label{FABL.FiniteDecisionTree.depth}
\leanok
\uses{FABL.FiniteDecisionTree}
Let $\Omega$ be finite, and let $T$ be a finite decision tree with alphabet $\Omega$ and
labels $\alpha$. Its depth is $0$ for a leaf; at a query, its depth is one plus the
maximum depth among the child trees indexed by answers in $\Omega$.
\end{definition}

\begin{definition}[Whether a coordinate is queried]
\lean{FABL.FiniteDecisionTree.Queries}
\label{FABL.FiniteDecisionTree.Queries}
\leanok
\uses{FABL.FiniteAlphabetDecisionTree, FABL.FiniteDecisionTree.queryTrace}
Let $T$ be a finite alphabet decision tree on $n$ coordinates with alphabet $Ω$, let $i$
be one of its coordinates, and let $x$ assign an alphabet symbol to every coordinate.
The tree queries $i$ on input $x$ exactly when $i$ appears in the query trace of $T$ on
$x$.
\end{definition}

Let $\Omega$ and $\alpha$ be types, let $n$ be a natural number, and let a finite
decision tree have its queries restricted to an available set
$A\subseteq\{0,\ldots,n-1\}$. For every input $x:\{0,\ldots,n-1\}\to\Omega$, each
coordinate in the tree's query trace belongs to $A$.
\end{theorem}

\begin{theorem}[Query set cardinality equals query count]
\lean{FABL.FiniteDecisionTree.card_querySet_eq_queryCount}
\label{FABL.FiniteDecisionTree.card_querySet_eq_queryCount}
\leanok

of distinct coordinates queried by $T$ on $x$ equals the length of its query trace.
\end{theorem}

\begin{theorem}[Query count bounded by available coordinates]
\lean{FABL.FiniteDecisionTree.queryCount_le_card_available}
\label{FABL.FiniteDecisionTree.queryCount_le_card_available}
\leanok
\uses{FABL.FiniteDecisionTree, FABL.FiniteDecisionTree.card_querySet_eq_queryCount, FABL.FiniteDecisionTree.queryCount, FABL.FiniteDecisionTree.querySet, FABL.FiniteDecisionTree.queryTrace_subset_available}
\difficulty{3}
Let $n$ be a natural number, let $\Omega$ and $\alpha$ be types, and let
$A\subseteq\{0,\ldots,n-1\}$ be a set of available coordinates. For any finite decision
tree $T$ with available set $A$ and any input $x:\{0,\ldots,n-1\}\to\Omega$, the number
of queries made by $T$ on $x$ is at most $|A|$.
\end{theorem}

\begin{theorem}[Query count bounded by dimension]
\lean{FABL.FiniteDecisionTree.queryCount_le_dimension}
\label{FABL.FiniteDecisionTree.queryCount_le_dimension}

decision tree whose available coordinates are all of $\{0,\ldots,n-1\}$. For any input

\end{theorem}

\begin{theorem}[Query count bounded by tree depth]
\lean{FABL.FiniteDecisionTree.queryCount_le_depth}
\label{FABL.FiniteDecisionTree.queryCount_le_depth}

Let $n$ be a natural number, let $\Omega$ be a finite type, and let $\alpha$ be a type.
For any finite decision tree $T$ with available coordinates among $\{0,\ldots,n-1\}$ and
any input $x:\{0,\ldots,n-1\}\to\Omega$, the number of queries made by $T$ on $x$ is at
most its depth, where depth is the maximum number of queries along any branch.
\end{theorem}

\begin{theorem}[Depth bounded by available coordinates]

\begin{theorem}[Depth bounded by dimension]
\lean{FABL.FiniteDecisionTree.depth_le_dimension}

\begin{definition}[Decision tree computes a function]
\lean{FABL.FiniteDecisionTree.Computes}
\statementsource{Analysis-of-Boolean-Functions-by-Ryan-ODonnell}{
  pdf-ffbe9c7b3306-p073-b004,
  pdf-ffbe9c7b3306-p094-b006,
  pdf-ffbe9c7b3306-p230-b001
}
\label{FABL.FiniteDecisionTree.Computes}
\leanok
\uses{FABL.FiniteDecisionTree, FABL.FiniteDecisionTree.eval}
A finite decision tree $T$ with alphabet $\Omega$, labels $\alpha$, and available
coordinates $A\subseteq\{0,\ldots,n-1\}$ computes a function $f:\Omega^n\to\alpha$ if
evaluating $T$ gives $f(x)$ for every input $x\in\Omega^n$.
\end{definition}

\begin{theorem}[Pointwise characterization of computation]
\lean{FABL.FiniteDecisionTree.computes_iff}
\label{FABL.FiniteDecisionTree.computes_iff}
\leanok
\uses{FABL.FiniteDecisionTree, FABL.FiniteDecisionTree.Computes, FABL.FiniteDecisionTree.eval}
\difficulty{1}
Let $A$ be a set of available coordinates among $n$ coordinates, let $T$ be a decision
tree over $A$, and let $f:\Omega^n\to\alpha$. The tree computes $f$ if and only if, for
every input $x\in\Omega^n$, evaluating $T$ at $x$ gives $f(x)$.
\end{theorem}

\begin{theorem}[Query indicators sum to the query count]
\lean{FABL.FiniteDecisionTree.sum_queryIndicator_eq_queryCount}
\label{FABL.FiniteDecisionTree.sum_queryIndicator_eq_queryCount}
\leanok
\uses{FABL.FiniteAlphabetDecisionTree, FABL.FiniteDecisionTree.Queries, FABL.FiniteDecisionTree.card_querySet_eq_queryCount, FABL.FiniteDecisionTree.queryCount, FABL.FiniteDecisionTree.querySet}
\difficulty{4}
Let $T$ be a finite-alphabet decision tree on all $n$ coordinates, and let $x$ be an
input. The sum over all coordinates of the indicator that the coordinate occurs in the
query trace of $T$ on $x$ equals the length of that trace, which is the query count.
\end{theorem}

\begin{definition}[Embedding binary decision trees]
\lean{FABL.FiniteDecisionTree.ofF₂DecisionTree}
\leanok
\uses{FABL.FiniteDecisionTree, FABL.F₂DecisionTree}
For any finite set of available coordinates, a decision tree whose queries have two
children, labelled by the bit values $0$ and $1$, determines a decision tree over the
alphabet $\bbr/\bbr?$. Here the child for $0$ is selected when the queried value is zero,
and the child for $1$ otherwise.
\end{definition}

\begin{theorem}[Evaluation of a binary tree conversion]
\lean{FABL.FiniteDecisionTree.eval_ofF₂DecisionTree}
\leanok
\uses{FABL.FiniteDecisionTree.eval, FABL.FiniteDecisionTree.ofF₂DecisionTree, FABL.F₂DecisionTree, FABL.F₂DecisionTree.eval}
\difficulty{4}
Let $T$ be a binary decision tree on $n$ coordinates with labels in a type $\alpha$, and
let $x$ assign an element of $\mathbb{Z}/2\mathbb{Z}$ to each coordinate. Evaluating the
finite-alphabet decision tree over $\mathbb{Z}/2\mathbb{Z}$ obtained from $T$ gives the
same label as evaluating $T$ at $x$.
\end{theorem}

\begin{definition}[Completing a decision tree recursively]
\lean{FABL.FiniteDecisionTree.completeTreeAux}
\label{FABL.FiniteDecisionTree.completeTreeAux}
\leanok
\uses{FABL.FiniteDecisionTree}
Let $a9$ be a nonempty alphabet, let $f:(\text{Fin }n\toa9)\to\mathbb1$ be a function, and let
$x$ be a partial input and $A$ a finite set of available coordinates. The recursively
defined tree queries the least coordinate of $A$, branching on each alphabet value and
continuing with that coordinate updated in $x$; when $A$ is empty, it returns $f(x)$.
\end{definition}

\begin{theorem}[Evaluation of the completed decision tree]
\lean{FABL.FiniteDecisionTree.eval_completeTreeAux}
\label{FABL.FiniteDecisionTree.eval_completeTreeAux}
\leanok
\uses{FABL.FiniteDecisionTree.completeTreeAux, FABL.FiniteDecisionTree.eval}
\difficulty{6}
Let $\Omega$ be a nonempty alphabet, let $f$ map inputs on $n$ coordinates over $\Omega$
to $\alpha$, and let $u$ and $x$ be two such inputs. Given a set $A$ of available
coordinates, suppose $u_i=x_i$ for every coordinate $i$ outside $A$. Then the tree
constructed from $f$, the partial input $u$, and the available set $A$ evaluates on $x$
to $f(x)$.
\end{theorem}

\begin{definition}[Complete decision tree for a function]
\lean{FABL.FiniteDecisionTree.completeTree}
\label{FABL.FiniteDecisionTree.completeTree}
\leanok
\uses{FABL.FiniteAlphabetDecisionTree, FABL.FiniteDecisionTree.completeTreeAux}
Let $a9$ be a nonempty alphabet and let $f:(\text{Fin }n\toa9)\to\mathbb1$. The complete
decision tree queries all coordinates, in increasing order, branching on their alphabet
values, and returns the value of $f$ on the resulting input.
\end{definition}

\begin{theorem}[Completeness of the canonical decision tree]
\lean{FABL.FiniteDecisionTree.completeTree_computes}
\label{FABL.FiniteDecisionTree.completeTree_computes}
\leanok
\uses{FABL.FiniteDecisionTree.Computes, FABL.FiniteDecisionTree.completeTree, FABL.FiniteDecisionTree.eval_completeTreeAux}
\difficulty{3}
Let $\Omega$ be a nonempty set, let $n$ be a natural number, and let
$f:\Omega^n\to\alpha$ be a function. The decision tree that queries all coordinates in
order and returns $f(x)$ at the leaf corresponding to input $x$ computes $f$ on every
input.
\end{theorem}

\begin{theorem}[Existence of a computing tree with a depth]
\lean{FABL.FiniteDecisionTree.exists_computingTree_with_depth}
\proofsource{Analysis-of-Boolean-Functions-by-Ryan-ODonnell}{pdf-ffbe9c7b3306-p087-b004}

\leanok

\difficulty{1}
Let $\Omega$ be a finite nonempty set, let $n$ be a natural number, let $\alpha$ be a
type, and let $f:(\mathrm{Fin}(n)\to\Omega)\to\alpha$. There exist a natural number $d$
and a decision tree that computes $f$ and has depth $d$.
\end{theorem}

\begin{definition}[Deterministic decision-tree depth]
\lean{FABL.FiniteDecisionTree.deterministicDepth}
\statementsource{Analysis-of-Boolean-Functions-by-Ryan-ODonnell}{
  pdf-ffbe9c7b3306-p014-b012,
  pdf-ffbe9c7b3306-p074-b002,

}
\label{FABL.FiniteDecisionTree.deterministicDepth}
\leanok
\uses{FABL.FiniteDecisionTree.exists_computingTree_with_depth}
Let $\Omega$ be a finite nonempty alphabet, let $n$ be a natural number, and let $f :
\Omega^n \to \alpha$ be a function. Its deterministic depth is the least depth of a
finite decision tree that computes $f$.
\end{definition}

\begin{theorem}[Tree attaining deterministic depth]
\lean{FABL.FiniteDecisionTree.exists_computingTree_depth_eq_deterministicDepth}
\label{FABL.FiniteDecisionTree.exists_computingTree_depth_eq_deterministicDepth}
\leanok
\uses{FABL.FiniteAlphabetDecisionTree, FABL.FiniteDecisionTree.Computes, FABL.FiniteDecisionTree.depth, FABL.FiniteDecisionTree.deterministicDepth, FABL.FiniteDecisionTree.exists_computingTree_with_depth}
\difficulty{2}
Let $\Omega$ be a finite nonempty set, let $n$ be a natural number, let $\alpha$ be a
type, and let $f:(\mathrm{Fin}(n)\to\Omega)\to\alpha$. There exists a decision tree that
computes $f$ and whose depth equals the least depth of any decision tree computing $f$.
\end{theorem}

\begin{theorem}[Minimal deterministic depth bound]
\lean{FABL.FiniteDecisionTree.deterministicDepth_le_of_computes}
\label{FABL.FiniteDecisionTree.deterministicDepth_le_of_computes}
\leanok
\uses{FABL.FiniteAlphabetDecisionTree, FABL.FiniteDecisionTree.Computes, FABL.FiniteDecisionTree.depth, FABL.FiniteDecisionTree.deterministicDepth, FABL.FiniteDecisionTree.exists_computingTree_with_depth}
\difficulty{2}
Let $\Omega$ be a finite nonempty alphabet, let $f:(\mathrm{Fin}(n)\to\Omega)\to\alpha$,
and let $T$ be a finite decision tree that computes $f$ on every input. The minimum
depth of a finite decision tree computing $f$ is at most the depth of $T$.
\end{theorem}

\begin{theorem}[Existence of a computing tree with a leaf count]
\lean{FABL.FiniteDecisionTree.exists_computingTree_with_leafCount}
\label{FABL.FiniteDecisionTree.exists_computingTree_with_leafCount}
\leanok
\uses{FABL.FiniteAlphabetDecisionTree, FABL.FiniteDecisionTree.Computes, FABL.FiniteDecisionTree.completeTree, FABL.FiniteDecisionTree.completeTree_computes, FABL.FiniteDecisionTree.leafCount}
\difficulty{1}
Let $\Omega$ be a finite nonempty set, let $n$ be a natural number, let $\alpha$ be a
type, and let $f:(\mathrm{Fin}(n)\to\Omega)\to\alpha$. There exist a natural number $s$
and a decision tree that computes $f$ and has exactly $s$ leaves.
\end{theorem}

\begin{definition}[Deterministic decision-tree size]
\lean{FABL.FiniteDecisionTree.deterministicSize}
\statementsource{Analysis-of-Boolean-Functions-by-Ryan-ODonnell}{
  pdf-ffbe9c7b3306-p014-b012,
  pdf-ffbe9c7b3306-p074-b002
}
\label{FABL.FiniteDecisionTree.deterministicSize}
\leanok
\uses{FABL.FiniteDecisionTree.exists_computingTree_with_leafCount}
Let $\Omega$ be a finite nonempty alphabet, let $n$ be a natural number, and let $f :
\Omega^n \to \alpha$ be a function. Its deterministic size is the least number of leaves
in a finite decision tree that computes $f$.
\end{definition}

\begin{definition}[Decision-tree process sample]
\lean{FABL.FiniteDecisionTree.ProcessSample}
\statementsource{Analysis-of-Boolean-Functions-by-Ryan-ODonnell}{pdf-ffbe9c7b3306-p234-b002}
\label{FABL.FiniteDecisionTree.ProcessSample}
\leanok
\uses{FABL.FiniteAlphabetDecisionTree, FABL.FiniteDecisionTree.queryTrace}
Let $T$ be a finite decision tree on inputs in $\Omega^n$. A process sample for $T$
consists of a final input $x \in \Omega^n$ and a list of queried coordinates that is
exactly the query trace of $T$ on $x$.
\end{definition}

\begin{definition}[Process sample from an input]
\lean{FABL.FiniteDecisionTree.ProcessSample.ofInput}
\label{FABL.FiniteDecisionTree.ProcessSample.ofInput}
\leanok
\uses{FABL.FiniteAlphabetDecisionTree, FABL.FiniteDecisionTree.ProcessSample, FABL.FiniteDecisionTree.queryTrace}
Given a finite alphabet decision tree and an input $x$, the associated process sample
consists of $x$ together with the ordered list of coordinates queried during the tree's
execution on $x$.
\end{definition}

\begin{definition}[Set of queried coordinates]
\lean{FABL.FiniteDecisionTree.ProcessSample.queriedSet}
\statementsource{Analysis-of-Boolean-Functions-by-Ryan-ODonnell}{pdf-ffbe9c7b3306-p234-b002}
\label{FABL.FiniteDecisionTree.ProcessSample.queriedSet}
\leanok
\uses{FABL.FiniteAlphabetDecisionTree, FABL.FiniteDecisionTree.ProcessSample}
Let $T$ be a finite decision tree on inputs in $\Omega^n$, and let a process sample for
$T$ have query trace $L$. Its queried set is the set of coordinates that occur in $L$.
\end{definition}

\begin{theorem}[No repeated queries in a decision tree trace]
\lean{FABL.FiniteDecisionTree.ProcessSample.trace_nodup}
\label{FABL.FiniteDecisionTree.ProcessSample.trace_nodup}
\leanok
\uses{FABL.FiniteAlphabetDecisionTree, FABL.FiniteDecisionTree.ProcessSample, FABL.FiniteDecisionTree.queryTrace_nodup}
\difficulty{3}
Let $T$ be a finite decision tree on $n$ coordinates, and let a process sample consist
of an input $x\in\Omega^n$ and a trace equal to the sequence of coordinates queried by
$T$ on $x$. Then no coordinate occurs more than once in the trace.
\end{theorem}

\begin{definition}[Decision-tree process distribution]
\lean{FABL.FiniteDecisionTree.decisionTreeProcessPMF}
\statementsource{Analysis-of-Boolean-Functions-by-Ryan-ODonnell}{pdf-ffbe9c7b3306-p234-b002}
\label{FABL.FiniteDecisionTree.decisionTreeProcessPMF}
\leanok
\uses{FABL.FiniteAlphabetDecisionTree, FABL.FiniteDecisionTree.ProcessSample, FABL.FiniteDecisionTree.ProcessSample.ofInput, FABL.productProbabilityPMF}
Let $\Omega$ be a finite alphabet, let $\pi$ be a probability distribution on $\Omega$,
and let $T$ be a finite decision tree on inputs in $\Omega^n$. The process distribution
of $T$ is the distribution of the process sample obtained by drawing each of the $n$
input coordinates independently according to $\pi$ and recording the resulting input and
its query trace.
\end{definition}

\begin{theorem}[Input marginal of the tree process]
\lean{FABL.FiniteDecisionTree.decisionTreeProcessPMF_map_input}
\label{FABL.FiniteDecisionTree.decisionTreeProcessPMF_map_input}
\leanok
\uses{FABL.FiniteAlphabetDecisionTree, FABL.FiniteDecisionTree.ProcessSample.ofInput, FABL.FiniteDecisionTree.decisionTreeProcessPMF, FABL.productProbabilityPMF}
\difficulty{3}
Let $\Omega$ be finite, let $\pi$ be a probability distribution on $\Omega$, and let $T$
be a decision tree on $n$ coordinates. If a process sample is formed by drawing the
input from the product distribution $\pi^n$ and recording the tree's query trace, then
the marginal distribution of its input is $\pi^n$.
\end{theorem}

\begin{theorem}[Evaluation of a computed function]
\lean{FABL.FiniteDecisionTree.ProcessSample.eval_eq_of_computes}
\label{FABL.FiniteDecisionTree.ProcessSample.eval_eq_of_computes}
\leanok
\uses{FABL.FiniteAlphabetDecisionTree, FABL.FiniteDecisionTree.Computes, FABL.FiniteDecisionTree.ProcessSample, FABL.FiniteDecisionTree.eval}
\difficulty{1}
Let $T$ be a finite decision tree on $n$ coordinates over an alphabet $\Omega$, with
output alphabet $\alpha$, and let $f:(\mathrm{Fin}(n)\to\Omega)\to\alpha$. If evaluating
$T$ on any input gives $f$ of that input, then for any input together with a trace equal
to the sequence of coordinates queried by $T$ on that input, evaluating $T$ on the input
equals $f$ of the input.
\end{theorem}

\begin{definition}[Zero-error randomized decision tree]
\lean{FABL.RandomizedDecisionTree}
\statementsource{Analysis-of-Boolean-Functions-by-Ryan-ODonnell}{
  pdf-ffbe9c7b3306-p014-b009,
  pdf-ffbe9c7b3306-p230-b003
}
\label{FABL.RandomizedDecisionTree}
\leanok
\uses{FABL.FiniteAlphabetDecisionTree, FABL.FiniteDecisionTree.Computes}
Let $\Omega$ be an alphabet, let $\alpha$ be an output type, let $n$ be a natural
number, and let $f : \Omega^n \to \alpha$. A zero-error randomized decision tree for $f$
consists of a finite nonempty seed space with a probability distribution, together with
a finite decision tree on $\Omega^n$ for each seed, such that every tree computes $f$ on
every input.
\end{definition}

\begin{definition}[Deterministic tree as a randomized tree]
\lean{FABL.RandomizedDecisionTree.ofDeterministic}
\label{FABL.RandomizedDecisionTree.ofDeterministic}
\leanok
\uses{FABL.FiniteAlphabetDecisionTree, FABL.FiniteDecisionTree.Computes, FABL.RandomizedDecisionTree}
Let a deterministic decision tree compute a function $f$ on inputs over a finite
alphabet. It defines a randomized decision tree for $f$ by using a singleton seed space,
assigning that seed probability one, and selecting the given tree.
\end{definition}

\begin{definition}[Distribution of selected trees]
\lean{FABL.RandomizedDecisionTree.treePMF}
\statementsource{Analysis-of-Boolean-Functions-by-Ryan-ODonnell}{pdf-ffbe9c7b3306-p230-b003}
\label{FABL.RandomizedDecisionTree.treePMF}
\leanok
\uses{FABL.FiniteAlphabetDecisionTree, FABL.RandomizedDecisionTree}
Let a randomized decision tree have seed distribution $\mu$ and assign a deterministic
tree $T_s$ to each seed $s$. The distribution of its selected tree is the probability
distribution obtained by sampling $s$ according to $\mu$ and returning $T_s$.
\end{definition}

Let $T$ be a randomized decision tree computing a function $f$ on inputs of length $n$,
and let $S$ be a deterministic decision tree in the support of the distribution of trees
selected by $T$. Then $S$ computes $f$ on every input.
\end{theorem}

\begin{definition}[Expected query cost on an input]
\lean{FABL.RandomizedDecisionTree.inputCost}
\statementsource{Analysis-of-Boolean-Functions-by-Ryan-ODonnell}{
  pdf-ffbe9c7b3306-p014-b009,
  pdf-ffbe9c7b3306-p230-b003
}
\label{FABL.RandomizedDecisionTree.inputCost}
\leanok
\uses{FABL.FiniteDecisionTree.queryCount, FABL.RandomizedDecisionTree, FABL.pmfExpectation}
Let a randomized decision tree have seed distribution $\mu$, and fix an input $x \in
\Omega^n$. Its input cost at $x$ is the expected number of coordinates queried by the
selected tree on $x$, with expectation taken over the seed.
\end{definition}

\begin{definition}[Worst-case query cost]
\lean{FABL.RandomizedDecisionTree.worstCaseCost}
\statementsource{Analysis-of-Boolean-Functions-by-Ryan-ODonnell}{pdf-ffbe9c7b3306-p230-b003}
\label{FABL.RandomizedDecisionTree.worstCaseCost}
\leanok
\uses{FABL.RandomizedDecisionTree, FABL.RandomizedDecisionTree.inputCost}
Let a randomized decision tree have a finite, nonempty seed space, and suppose its
alphabet is finite and nonempty. Its worst-case cost is the supremum, over all seeds, of
the input cost of the deterministic tree selected by that seed.
\end{definition}

\begin{theorem}[Input cost bounded by worst-case cost]
\lean{FABL.RandomizedDecisionTree.inputCost_le_worstCaseCost}
\label{FABL.RandomizedDecisionTree.inputCost_le_worstCaseCost}
\leanok
\uses{FABL.RandomizedDecisionTree, FABL.RandomizedDecisionTree.inputCost, FABL.RandomizedDecisionTree.worstCaseCost}
\difficulty{1}
Let $\Omega$ be a finite nonempty set, let $\alpha$ be a type, let $n$ be a nonnegative
integer, and let $f:(Fin nto\Omega)to\alpha$. For every zero-error randomized
decision tree $T$ computing $f$ and every input $x$, the expected number of queries on
$x$ is at most the maximum expected query count over all inputs.
\end{theorem}

\begin{theorem}[Input cost bounded by dimension]
\lean{FABL.RandomizedDecisionTree.inputCost_le_dimension}
\label{FABL.RandomizedDecisionTree.inputCost_le_dimension}
\leanok
\uses{FABL.FiniteDecisionTree.queryCount, FABL.FiniteDecisionTree.queryCount_le_dimension, FABL.RandomizedDecisionTree, FABL.RandomizedDecisionTree.inputCost, FABL.pmfExpectation}
\difficulty{4}
Let $n$ be a nonnegative integer, let $\Omega$ and $\alpha$ be types, let $f:(Fin
nto\Omega)to\alpha$, and let $T$ be a zero-error randomized decision tree computing
$f$. For every input $x:(Fin nto\Omega)$, the expected number of coordinates queried
by $T$ on $x$ is at most $n$.
\end{theorem}

\begin{definition}[Query probability on an input]
\lean{FABL.RandomizedDecisionTree.queryProbabilityOnInput}
\label{FABL.RandomizedDecisionTree.queryProbabilityOnInput}
\leanok
\uses{FABL.FiniteDecisionTree.Queries, FABL.RandomizedDecisionTree, FABL.pmfExpectation}
For a randomized decision tree, a coordinate $i$, and an input $x$, the query
probability is the expected indicator, over the random seed, that the selected
deterministic tree queries $i$ on $x$.
\end{definition}

\begin{definition}[Coordinate query probability]
\lean{FABL.RandomizedDecisionTree.queryProbability}
\statementsource{Analysis-of-Boolean-Functions-by-Ryan-ODonnell}{
  pdf-ffbe9c7b3306-p014-b009,
  pdf-ffbe9c7b3306-p230-b005
}
\label{FABL.RandomizedDecisionTree.queryProbability}
\leanok
\uses{FABL.RandomizedDecisionTree, FABL.RandomizedDecisionTree.queryProbabilityOnInput, FABL.pmfExpectation, FABL.productProbabilityPMF}
Let a randomized decision tree have a finite alphabet, let $\pi$ be a probability
distribution on the alphabet, and let $i$ be a coordinate. The probability that the tree
queries coordinate $i$ is the expected probability of querying $i$ on an input whose $n$
coordinates are sampled independently from $\pi$.
\end{definition}

\begin{definition}[Average query cost]
\lean{FABL.RandomizedDecisionTree.averageCost}
\statementsource{Analysis-of-Boolean-Functions-by-Ryan-ODonnell}{
  pdf-ffbe9c7b3306-p014-b009,
  pdf-ffbe9c7b3306-p230-b005
}
\label{FABL.RandomizedDecisionTree.averageCost}
\leanok
\uses{FABL.RandomizedDecisionTree, FABL.RandomizedDecisionTree.inputCost, FABL.pmfExpectation, FABL.productProbabilityPMF}
Let a randomized decision tree have a finite alphabet, and let $\pi$ be a probability
distribution on that alphabet. Its average cost is the expected input cost when the $n$
input coordinates are sampled independently from $\pi$.
\end{definition}

\begin{theorem}[Nonnegativity of input cost]
\lean{FABL.RandomizedDecisionTree.inputCost_nonneg}
\label{FABL.RandomizedDecisionTree.inputCost_nonneg}
\leanok
\uses{FABL.RandomizedDecisionTree, FABL.RandomizedDecisionTree.inputCost, FABL.pmfExpectation_nonneg}
\difficulty{1}
Let $n$ be a nonnegative integer, let $\Omega$ and $\alpha$ be types, let $f:(Fin
nto\Omega)to\alpha$, and let $T$ be a zero-error randomized decision tree computing
$f$. For every input $x$, the expected number of queries made by $T$ on $x$ is
nonnegative.
\end{theorem}

\begin{theorem}[Nonnegativity of worst-case cost]
\lean{FABL.RandomizedDecisionTree.worstCaseCost_nonneg}
\label{FABL.RandomizedDecisionTree.worstCaseCost_nonneg}
\leanok
\uses{FABL.RandomizedDecisionTree, FABL.RandomizedDecisionTree.inputCost, FABL.RandomizedDecisionTree.inputCost_nonneg, FABL.RandomizedDecisionTree.worstCaseCost}
\difficulty{3}
Let the input alphabet be finite and nonempty, and let $T$ be a randomized decision tree
whose deterministic trees all compute the same function. Its worst-case expected number
of queries is nonnegative.
\end{theorem}

\begin{theorem}[Nonnegativity of average query cost]
\lean{FABL.RandomizedDecisionTree.averageCost_nonneg}
\label{FABL.RandomizedDecisionTree.averageCost_nonneg}
\leanok
\uses{FABL.RandomizedDecisionTree, FABL.RandomizedDecisionTree.averageCost, FABL.RandomizedDecisionTree.inputCost_nonneg, FABL.pmfExpectation_nonneg, FABL.productProbabilityPMF}
\difficulty{1}
For a finite input alphabet, any randomized decision tree and any probability
distribution on that alphabet have nonnegative average query cost.
\end{theorem}

\begin{theorem}[Nonnegativity of query probability]
\lean{FABL.RandomizedDecisionTree.queryProbability_nonneg}
\label{FABL.RandomizedDecisionTree.queryProbability_nonneg}
\leanok
\uses{FABL.RandomizedDecisionTree, FABL.RandomizedDecisionTree.queryProbability, FABL.pmfExpectation_nonneg}
\difficulty{4}
Let $\Omega$ be a finite input alphabet with probability law $\pi$, and let $T$ be a
randomized decision tree with finite nonempty seed space. For every coordinate $i$, the
probability that $T$ queries $i$ under independent inputs of law $\pi$ is nonnegative.
\end{theorem}

\begin{theorem}[Upper bound on query probability]
\lean{FABL.RandomizedDecisionTree.queryProbability_le_one}
\label{FABL.RandomizedDecisionTree.queryProbability_le_one}
\leanok
\uses{FABL.RandomizedDecisionTree, FABL.RandomizedDecisionTree.queryProbability, FABL.RandomizedDecisionTree.queryProbabilityOnInput, FABL.pmfExpectation, FABL.pmfExpectation_const_one, FABL.pmfExpectation_mono, FABL.productProbabilityPMF}
\difficulty{4}
Let $\Omega$ be a finite input alphabet with probability law $\pi$, and let $T$ be a
randomized decision tree with finite nonempty seed space. For every coordinate $i$, the
probability that $T$ queries $i$ under independent inputs of law $\pi$ is at most $1$.
\end{theorem}

\begin{definition}[Revealment]
\lean{FABL.RandomizedDecisionTree.revealment}
\statementsource{Analysis-of-Boolean-Functions-by-Ryan-ODonnell}{
  pdf-ffbe9c7b3306-p014-b009,
  pdf-ffbe9c7b3306-p230-b005
}
\label{FABL.RandomizedDecisionTree.revealment}
\leanok
\uses{FABL.RandomizedDecisionTree, FABL.RandomizedDecisionTree.queryProbability}
Let a randomized decision tree have a finite alphabet, and let $\pi$ be a probability
distribution on that alphabet. Its revealment is the largest probability, over the $n$
coordinates, that the tree queries that coordinate, with revealment defined to be $0$
when there are no coordinates.
\end{definition}

\begin{theorem}[Total query probability equals input cost]
\lean{FABL.RandomizedDecisionTree.sum_queryProbabilityOnInput_eq_inputCost}
\label{FABL.RandomizedDecisionTree.sum_queryProbabilityOnInput_eq_inputCost}
\leanok
\uses{FABL.FiniteDecisionTree.Queries, FABL.FiniteDecisionTree.queryCount, FABL.FiniteDecisionTree.sum_queryIndicator_eq_queryCount, FABL.RandomizedDecisionTree, FABL.RandomizedDecisionTree.inputCost, FABL.RandomizedDecisionTree.queryProbabilityOnInput, FABL.pmfExpectation, FABL.pmfExpectation_sum}
\difficulty{4}
Let $n$ be a natural number, let $\Omega$ and $\alpha$ be types, let
$f:\Omega^n\to\alpha$, and let $T$ be a randomized decision tree computing $f$, with a
finite nonempty seed space and a probability law on its seeds. For every input
$x\in\Omega^n$, the sum over all coordinates of the probability that $T$ queries that
coordinate on $x$ equals the expected number of queries made on $x$.
\end{theorem}

\begin{theorem}[Sum query probability eq average cost]
\lean{FABL.RandomizedDecisionTree.sum_queryProbability_eq_averageCost}

\begin{theorem}[Average cost bounded by worst-case cost]
\lean{FABL.RandomizedDecisionTree.averageCost_le_worstCaseCost}
\label{FABL.RandomizedDecisionTree.averageCost_le_worstCaseCost}
\leanok
\uses{FABL.RandomizedDecisionTree, FABL.RandomizedDecisionTree.averageCost, FABL.RandomizedDecisionTree.inputCost_le_worstCaseCost, FABL.RandomizedDecisionTree.worstCaseCost, FABL.pmfExpectation, FABL.pmfExpectation_const, FABL.pmfExpectation_mono, FABL.productProbabilityPMF}
\difficulty{3}
Let $n$ be a nonnegative integer, let $\\Omega$ be a finite nonempty input alphabet with
probability distribution $\\pi$, let $\\alpha$ be an output set, and let
$f:\\Omega^n\\to\\alpha$. For any randomized decision tree $T$ computing $f$, its
average query cost under independent inputs drawn from $\\pi$ is at most its worst-case
query cost over all inputs.
\end{theorem}

\begin{theorem}[Revealment bounded by average cost]
\lean{FABL.RandomizedDecisionTree.revealment_le_averageCost}
\label{FABL.RandomizedDecisionTree.revealment_le_averageCost}
\leanok
\uses{FABL.RandomizedDecisionTree, FABL.RandomizedDecisionTree.averageCost, FABL.RandomizedDecisionTree.averageCost_nonneg, FABL.RandomizedDecisionTree.queryProbability, FABL.RandomizedDecisionTree.queryProbability_nonneg, FABL.RandomizedDecisionTree.revealment, FABL.RandomizedDecisionTree.sum_queryProbability_eq_averageCost}
\difficulty{4}
Let $n$ be a nonnegative integer, let $\Omega$ be a finite input alphabet, and let $T$
be a randomized decision tree on $n$ coordinates with a finite nonempty seed space and a
probability law on its seeds, such that every seed selects a tree computing the same
function. For any probability distribution $\pi$ on $\Omega$, the largest, over
coordinates, of the probability that the tree queries that coordinate on an independent
product-distributed input is at most the expected number of queries under that input
distribution.
\end{theorem}

\begin{theorem}[Coordinate query probability bounded by revealment]
\lean{FABL.RandomizedDecisionTree.queryProbability_le_revealment}
\label{FABL.RandomizedDecisionTree.queryProbability_le_revealment}
\leanok
\uses{FABL.RandomizedDecisionTree, FABL.RandomizedDecisionTree.queryProbability, FABL.RandomizedDecisionTree.revealment}
\difficulty{3}
Let $\Omega$ be a finite input alphabet with probability law $\pi$, and let $T$ be a
randomized decision tree with finite nonempty seed space. For every coordinate $i$, its
probability of being queried under independent inputs of law $\pi$ is at most the
revealment of $T$ under $\pi$, defined as the maximum query probability over all
coordinates, or $0$ if there are no coordinates.
\end{theorem}

\begin{theorem}[Average cost and revealment]
\lean{FABL.RandomizedDecisionTree.averageCost_le_card_mul_revealment}
\label{FABL.RandomizedDecisionTree.averageCost_le_card_mul_revealment}
\leanok
\uses{FABL.RandomizedDecisionTree, FABL.RandomizedDecisionTree.averageCost, FABL.RandomizedDecisionTree.queryProbability, FABL.RandomizedDecisionTree.queryProbability_le_revealment, FABL.RandomizedDecisionTree.revealment, FABL.RandomizedDecisionTree.sum_queryProbability_eq_averageCost}
\difficulty{3}
Let $n$ be a nonnegative integer, let $\\Omega$ be a finite input alphabet with
probability distribution $\\pi$, and let $T$ be a randomized decision tree on $n$
coordinates. For each coordinate, consider the probability—over both the product input
distribution and the tree's random seed—that the tree queries it, and let the largest
such probability be zero if there are no coordinates. The average query cost is at most
$n$ times this largest probability.
\end{theorem}

\begin{definition}[Equal query probabilities]
\lean{FABL.RandomizedDecisionTree.HasEqualQueryProbabilities}
\label{FABL.RandomizedDecisionTree.HasEqualQueryProbabilities}
\leanok
\uses{FABL.RandomizedDecisionTree, FABL.RandomizedDecisionTree.queryProbability}
For a randomized decision tree over a finite alphabet and a probability distribution
$\bbc0$ on that alphabet, equal query probabilities means that every pair of coordinates
has the same query probability under $\bbc0$.
\end{definition}

\begin{theorem}[Revealment under equal query probabilities]
\lean{FABL.RandomizedDecisionTree.revealment_eq_averageCost_div}
\label{FABL.RandomizedDecisionTree.revealment_eq_averageCost_div}
\leanok
\uses{FABL.RandomizedDecisionTree, FABL.RandomizedDecisionTree.HasEqualQueryProbabilities, FABL.RandomizedDecisionTree.averageCost, FABL.RandomizedDecisionTree.queryProbability, FABL.RandomizedDecisionTree.revealment, FABL.RandomizedDecisionTree.sum_queryProbability_eq_averageCost}
\difficulty{4}
Let $\Omega$ be a finite input alphabet with probability law $\pi$, and let $T$ be a
randomized decision tree with finite nonempty seed space on $n>0$ coordinates. Suppose
every coordinate has the same query probability under independent inputs of law $\pi$.
Then the revealment of $T$ equals its average number of queries divided by $n$.
\end{theorem}

\begin{definition}[Deterministic average query count]
\lean{FABL.RandomizedDecisionTree.deterministicAverageCost}
\statementsource{Analysis-of-Boolean-Functions-by-Ryan-ODonnell}{pdf-ffbe9c7b3306-p230-b004}
\label{FABL.RandomizedDecisionTree.deterministicAverageCost}
\leanok
\uses{FABL.FiniteAlphabetDecisionTree, FABL.FiniteDecisionTree.queryCount, FABL.pmfExpectation, FABL.productProbabilityPMF}
Let $\pi$ be a probability distribution on a finite alphabet, and let $T$ be a
deterministic decision tree on $n$ coordinates. The average cost of $T$ is the expected
number of coordinates queried when the input coordinates are sampled independently from
$\pi$.
\end{definition}

\begin{theorem}[Average cost as seed expectation]
\lean{FABL.RandomizedDecisionTree.averageCost_eq_seedExpectation}
\label{FABL.RandomizedDecisionTree.averageCost_eq_seedExpectation}
\leanok
\uses{FABL.RandomizedDecisionTree, FABL.RandomizedDecisionTree.averageCost, FABL.RandomizedDecisionTree.deterministicAverageCost, FABL.RandomizedDecisionTree.inputCost, FABL.pmfExpectation}
\difficulty{3}
Let $n$ be a nonnegative integer, let $\\Omega$ be a finite input alphabet with
probability distribution $\\pi$, let $\\alpha$ be an output set, and let
$f:\\Omega^n\\to\\alpha$. For any randomized decision tree $T$ computing $f$, its
average query cost under independent inputs drawn from $\\pi$ equals the expectation,
over the random seed of $T$, of the selected deterministic tree's average query cost
under that same input distribution.
\end{theorem}

\begin{theorem}[Average cost of a deterministic tree]
\lean{FABL.RandomizedDecisionTree.averageCost_ofDeterministic}
\label{FABL.RandomizedDecisionTree.averageCost_ofDeterministic}
\leanok
\uses{FABL.FiniteAlphabetDecisionTree, FABL.FiniteDecisionTree.Computes, FABL.RandomizedDecisionTree.averageCost, FABL.RandomizedDecisionTree.averageCost_eq_seedExpectation, FABL.RandomizedDecisionTree.deterministicAverageCost, FABL.RandomizedDecisionTree.ofDeterministic, FABL.pmfExpectation_pure}
\difficulty{3}
Let a finite input alphabet, a probability distribution on it, and a deterministic
decision tree computing a function be given. The randomized decision tree that selects
this deterministic tree with probability one has average query cost equal to the
deterministic tree’s average query cost.
\end{theorem}

\begin{theorem}[Deterministic Input Cost]
\lean{FABL.RandomizedDecisionTree.inputCost_ofDeterministic}
\label{FABL.RandomizedDecisionTree.inputCost_ofDeterministic}
\leanok
\uses{FABL.FiniteAlphabetDecisionTree, FABL.FiniteDecisionTree.Computes, FABL.FiniteDecisionTree.queryCount, FABL.RandomizedDecisionTree.inputCost, FABL.RandomizedDecisionTree.ofDeterministic, FABL.pmfExpectation_pure}
\difficulty{1}
Let $T$ be a finite decision tree on $n$ coordinates that computes a function $f$, and
let $x$ be an input. The expected number of queries made by the randomized tree obtained
by choosing $T$ deterministically, on input $x$, equals the number of queries made by
$T$ on $x$.
\end{theorem}

\begin{theorem}[Cost bound for deterministic trees]
\lean{FABL.RandomizedDecisionTree.worstCaseCost_ofDeterministic_le_depth}
\label{FABL.RandomizedDecisionTree.worstCaseCost_ofDeterministic_le_depth}
\leanok
\uses{FABL.FiniteAlphabetDecisionTree, FABL.FiniteDecisionTree.Computes, FABL.FiniteDecisionTree.depth, FABL.FiniteDecisionTree.queryCount_le_depth, FABL.RandomizedDecisionTree.inputCost_ofDeterministic, FABL.RandomizedDecisionTree.ofDeterministic, FABL.RandomizedDecisionTree.worstCaseCost}
\difficulty{3}
Let the input alphabet be finite and nonempty, and let $T$ be a deterministic decision
tree that computes $f$. Regard $T$ as a randomized decision tree with a single
deterministic choice. Its worst-case expected number of queries is at most the depth of
$T$.
\end{theorem}

\begin{theorem}[A deterministic tree with bounded average cost]
\lean{FABL.RandomizedDecisionTree.exists_deterministic_averageCost_le}
\label{FABL.RandomizedDecisionTree.exists_deterministic_averageCost_le}
\leanok
\uses{FABL.RandomizedDecisionTree, FABL.RandomizedDecisionTree.averageCost, FABL.RandomizedDecisionTree.averageCost_eq_seedExpectation, FABL.RandomizedDecisionTree.deterministicAverageCost, FABL.pmfExpectation_eq_integral}
\difficulty{4}
Let the input alphabet be finite. For every randomized decision tree and every
probability distribution on the input alphabet, there is a seed whose selected
deterministic tree has average query cost at most the randomized tree’s average query
cost.
\end{theorem}

\begin{definition}[Randomized decision-tree complexity]
\lean{FABL.RandomizedDecisionTree.complexity}
\statementsource{Analysis-of-Boolean-Functions-by-Ryan-ODonnell}{pdf-ffbe9c7b3306-p230-b003}
\label{FABL.RandomizedDecisionTree.complexity}
\leanok
\uses{FABL.RandomizedDecisionTree, FABL.RandomizedDecisionTree.worstCaseCost}
Let $f$ be a function on inputs of length $n$ over a finite, nonempty alphabet. Its
randomized decision-tree complexity is the infimum of the worst-case costs of randomized
decision trees that compute $f$ with zero error.
\end{definition}

\begin{definition}[Average randomized complexity]
\lean{FABL.RandomizedDecisionTree.averageComplexity}
\statementsource{Analysis-of-Boolean-Functions-by-Ryan-ODonnell}{pdf-ffbe9c7b3306-p230-b005}
\label{FABL.RandomizedDecisionTree.averageComplexity}
\leanok
\uses{FABL.RandomizedDecisionTree, FABL.RandomizedDecisionTree.averageCost}
Let $f$ be a function on inputs of length $n$ over a finite alphabet, and let $\pi$ be a
probability distribution on that alphabet. Its average randomized complexity is the
infimum of the average costs, under independent sampling from $\pi$, of randomized
decision trees that compute $f$ with zero error.
\end{definition}

\begin{definition}[Function revealment]
\lean{FABL.RandomizedDecisionTree.functionRevealment}
\statementsource{Analysis-of-Boolean-Functions-by-Ryan-ODonnell}{pdf-ffbe9c7b3306-p231-b002}
\label{FABL.RandomizedDecisionTree.functionRevealment}
\leanok
\uses{FABL.RandomizedDecisionTree, FABL.RandomizedDecisionTree.revealment}
Let $f$ be a function on inputs of length $n$ over a finite alphabet, and let $\pi$ be a
probability distribution on that alphabet. The function revealment is the infimum, over
randomized decision trees that compute $f$ with zero error, of their revealments under
$\pi$.
\end{definition}

\begin{theorem}[Nonnegativity of randomized complexity]
\lean{FABL.RandomizedDecisionTree.complexity_nonneg}
\label{FABL.RandomizedDecisionTree.complexity_nonneg}
\leanok
\uses{FABL.FiniteDecisionTree.completeTree, FABL.FiniteDecisionTree.completeTree_computes, FABL.RandomizedDecisionTree.complexity, FABL.RandomizedDecisionTree.ofDeterministic, FABL.RandomizedDecisionTree.worstCaseCost, FABL.RandomizedDecisionTree.worstCaseCost_nonneg}
\difficulty{4}
Let the input alphabet be finite and nonempty, and let $f$ be a function from length-$n$
inputs over this alphabet to an output alphabet. The randomized decision-tree complexity
of $f$ is nonnegative.
\end{theorem}

  {pdf-ffbe9c7b3306-p231-b003}
Let the input alphabet be finite and nonempty, and let $f$ be a function from length-$n$
inputs over this alphabet to an output alphabet. The randomized decision-tree complexity
of $f$ is at most the least depth of a deterministic decision tree computing $f$.
\end{theorem}

\begin{theorem}[Nonnegative average complexity]
\lean{FABL.RandomizedDecisionTree.averageComplexity_nonneg}
\label{FABL.RandomizedDecisionTree.averageComplexity_nonneg}
\leanok
\uses{FABL.FiniteDecisionTree.completeTree, FABL.FiniteDecisionTree.completeTree_computes, FABL.RandomizedDecisionTree.averageComplexity, FABL.RandomizedDecisionTree.averageCost, FABL.RandomizedDecisionTree.averageCost_nonneg, FABL.RandomizedDecisionTree.ofDeterministic}
\difficulty{4}
Let $n$ be a nonnegative integer, let $\\Omega$ be a finite input alphabet with
probability distribution $\\pi$, let $\\alpha$ be an output set, and let
$f:\\Omega^n\\to\\alpha$. The infimum of the average query costs, under independent
inputs drawn from $\\pi$, of all finite randomized decision trees that compute $f$ is
nonnegative.
\end{theorem}

\begin{definition}[Three-coordinate majority tree]
\lean{FABL.majorityThreePairTree}
\statementsource{Analysis-of-Boolean-Functions-by-Ryan-ODonnell}{pdf-ffbe9c7b3306-p230-b001}
\label{FABL.majorityThreePairTree}
\leanok
\uses{FABL.FiniteAlphabetDecisionTree, FABL.Sign}
Let $i,j,k$ be pairwise distinct coordinates in $\text{Fin}(3)$, and let each coordinate
take values in $\{-1,1	he same as sign\text{?}$
\end{definition}

\begin{definition}[Majority tree querying coordinates zero and one]
\lean{FABL.majorityThreeTree01}
\statementsource{Analysis-of-Boolean-Functions-by-Ryan-ODonnell}{pdf-ffbe9c7b3306-p230-b001}
\label{FABL.majorityThreeTree01}
\leanok
\uses{FABL.FiniteAlphabetDecisionTree, FABL.Sign, FABL.majorityThreePairTree}
For inputs in $\text{Fin}(3)$ with values in $␀$, define the tree that queries coordinate
$0$, then coordinate $1$, and returns their common value if they agree; otherwise it
queries coordinate $2$ and returns that value.
\end{definition}

\begin{definition}[Majority tree querying coordinates zero and two]
\lean{FABL.majorityThreeTree02}
\statementsource{Analysis-of-Boolean-Functions-by-Ryan-ODonnell}{pdf-ffbe9c7b3306-p230-b001}
\label{FABL.majorityThreeTree02}
\leanok
\uses{FABL.FiniteAlphabetDecisionTree, FABL.Sign, FABL.majorityThreePairTree}
For inputs in $\text{Fin}(3)$ with values in the integer units, define the tree that
queries coordinate $0$, then coordinate $2$, and returns their common value if they
agree; otherwise it queries coordinate $1$ and returns that value.
\end{definition}

\begin{definition}[Majority tree querying coordinates one and two]
\lean{FABL.majorityThreeTree12}
\statementsource{Analysis-of-Boolean-Functions-by-Ryan-ODonnell}{pdf-ffbe9c7b3306-p230-b001}
\label{FABL.majorityThreeTree12}
\leanok
\uses{FABL.FiniteAlphabetDecisionTree, FABL.Sign, FABL.majorityThreePairTree}
For inputs in $\text{Fin}(3)$ with values in the integer units, define the tree that
queries coordinate $1$, then coordinate $2$, and returns their common value if they
agree; otherwise it queries coordinate $0$ and returns that value.
\end{definition}

For every input of three signs, the output of the decision tree that first queries
coordinate $0$ and then queries coordinate $1$ is the majority of the three input signs.
\end{theorem}

  {Analysis-of-Boolean-Functions-by-Ryan-ODonnell}
  {pdf-ffbe9c7b3306-p231-b003,
    pdf-ffbe9c7b3306-p230-b004}
For every input of three signs in $\{-1,1\}$, the decision tree that first queries
coordinates $0$ and $2$, and queries coordinate $1$ if those signs differ, returns the
sign of the sum of the three input signs, with a nonnegative sum assigned the value $1$.
\end{theorem}

For every input of three signs in $\{-1,1\}$, the decision tree that first queries
coordinates $1$ and $2$, and queries coordinate $0$ if those signs differ, returns the
sign of the sum of the three input signs, with a nonnegative sum assigned the value $1$.
\end{theorem}

\begin{definition}[Majority tree selected by a seed]
\lean{FABL.majorityThreeTreeBySeed}
\statementsource{Analysis-of-Boolean-Functions-by-Ryan-ODonnell}{pdf-ffbe9c7b3306-p230-b002}
\label{FABL.majorityThreeTreeBySeed}
\leanok
\uses{FABL.FiniteAlphabetDecisionTree, FABL.Sign, FABL.majorityThreeTree01, FABL.majorityThreeTree02, FABL.majorityThreeTree12}
For a seed in $\text{Fin}(3)$, define a decision tree as follows: seed $0$ selects the
tree that first queries coordinates $0$ and $1$, seed $1$ selects the tree that first
queries coordinates $0$ and $2$, and seed $2$ selects the tree that first queries
coordinates $1$ and $2$. Each tree returns the queried pair's common value when they
agree, and otherwise queries the remaining coordinate and returns its value.
\end{definition}

\begin{theorem}[Seed zero selects the first tree]
\lean{FABL.majorityThreeTreeBySeed_zero}
\label{FABL.majorityThreeTreeBySeed_zero}
\leanok
\uses{FABL.majorityThreeTree01, FABL.majorityThreeTreeBySeed}
\difficulty{1}
When the seed is $0$, the seeded three-sign decision tree is exactly the tree that
queries coordinates $0$ and $1$ first and coordinate $2$ if their signs differ.
\end{theorem}

\begin{theorem}[Seed one selects the second tree]
\lean{FABL.majorityThreeTreeBySeed_one}
\label{FABL.majorityThreeTreeBySeed_one}
\leanok
\uses{FABL.majorityThreeTree02, FABL.majorityThreeTreeBySeed}
\difficulty{1}
When the seed is $1$, the seeded three-sign decision tree is exactly the tree that
queries coordinates $0$ and $2$ first and coordinate $1$ if their signs differ.
\end{theorem}

\begin{theorem}[Seed two selects the third tree]
\lean{FABL.majorityThreeTreeBySeed_two}
\label{FABL.majorityThreeTreeBySeed_two}
\leanok
\uses{FABL.majorityThreeTree12, FABL.majorityThreeTreeBySeed}
\difficulty{3}
When the seed is $2$, the seeded three-sign decision tree is exactly the tree that
queries coordinates $1$ and $2$ first and coordinate $0$ if their signs differ.
\end{theorem}

\begin{theorem}[Correctness of a seeded majority tree]
\lean{FABL.majorityThreeTreeBySeed_computes}
\label{FABL.majorityThreeTreeBySeed_computes}
\leanok
\uses{FABL.FiniteDecisionTree.Computes, FABL.majority, FABL.majorityThreeTree01_computes, FABL.majorityThreeTree02_computes, FABL.majorityThreeTree12_computes, FABL.majorityThreeTreeBySeed}
\difficulty{4}
For every seed among $0,1,2$ and every input of three signs in $\{-1,1\}$, choose the
tree that queries the two coordinates other than the seed first, and queries the seed if
those two signs differ. This tree returns the sign of the sum of the three input signs,
with a nonnegative sum assigned the value $1$.
\end{theorem}

\begin{definition}[Randomized three-coordinate majority tree]
\lean{FABL.majorityThreeRandomizedTree}
\statementsource{Analysis-of-Boolean-Functions-by-Ryan-ODonnell}{pdf-ffbe9c7b3306-p230-b002}
\label{FABL.majorityThreeRandomizedTree}
\leanok
\uses{FABL.RandomizedDecisionTree, FABL.Sign, FABL.majority, FABL.majorityThreeTreeBySeed, FABL.majorityThreeTreeBySeed_computes, FABL.uniformPMF}
There is a randomized decision tree for majority on three inputs taking values in
$\\{-1,1\}$. Its seed is uniform on the three-element set $\text{Fin}(3)$, and each seed
selects the corresponding pair-first tree; every selected tree computes majority exactly
on every input.
\end{definition}

\begin{theorem}[Query count of the first majority tree]
\lean{FABL.queryCount_majorityThreeTree01}
\label{FABL.queryCount_majorityThreeTree01}
\leanok
\uses{FABL.FiniteDecisionTree.queryCount, FABL.FiniteDecisionTree.queryTrace, FABL.SignCube, FABL.majorityThreePairTree, FABL.majorityThreeTree01}
\difficulty{4}
For every sign-valued input $x$ on three coordinates, the first majority tree makes two
queries when $x_0=x_1$ and three queries when $x_0\ne x_1$.
\end{theorem}

\begin{theorem}[Query count of the second majority tree]
\lean{FABL.queryCount_majorityThreeTree02}
\label{FABL.queryCount_majorityThreeTree02}
\leanok
\uses{FABL.FiniteDecisionTree.queryCount, FABL.FiniteDecisionTree.queryTrace, FABL.SignCube, FABL.majorityThreePairTree, FABL.majorityThreeTree02}
\difficulty{4}
For every sign-valued input $x$ on three coordinates, the second majority tree makes two
queries when $x_0=x_2$ and three queries when $x_0\ne x_2$.
\end{theorem}

\begin{theorem}[Query count of the third majority tree]
\lean{FABL.queryCount_majorityThreeTree12}
\label{FABL.queryCount_majorityThreeTree12}
\leanok
\uses{FABL.FiniteDecisionTree.queryCount, FABL.FiniteDecisionTree.queryTrace, FABL.SignCube, FABL.majorityThreePairTree, FABL.majorityThreeTree12}
\difficulty{4}
For every sign-valued input $x$ on three coordinates, the third majority tree makes two
queries when $x_1=x_2$ and three queries when $x_1\ne x_2$.
\end{theorem}

For every input $x\in\{−1,1\}^3$, the randomized decision tree's expected number of
queries is $\frac{1}{3}\bigl((2\text{ if }x_0=x_1\text{, and }3\text{
otherwise})+(2\text{ if }x_0=x_2\text{, and }3\text{ otherwise})+(2\text{ if
}x_1=x_2\text{, and }3\text{ otherwise})\bigr)$.
\end{theorem}

\begin{theorem}[Expected Query Cost Bound]
\lean{FABL.majorityThreeRandomizedTree_inputCost_le}
\label{FABL.majorityThreeRandomizedTree_inputCost_le}
\leanok
\uses{FABL.RandomizedDecisionTree.inputCost, FABL.SignCube, FABL.majorityThreeRandomizedTree, FABL.majorityThreeRandomizedTree_inputCost}
\difficulty{5}
For every input $x\in\{−1,1\}^3$, the randomized decision tree's expected number of
queries is at most $8/3$.
\end{theorem}

\begin{definition}[A worst input for three-coordinate majority]
\lean{FABL.majorityThreeWorstInput}
\label{FABL.majorityThreeWorstInput}
\leanok
\uses{FABL.SignCube}
Define a sign vector of length three by assigning $-1$ to coordinate $2$ and $1$ to each
other coordinate.
\end{definition}

\begin{theorem}[Cost on a Specified Input]
\lean{FABL.majorityThreeRandomizedTree_worstInputCost}
\label{FABL.majorityThreeRandomizedTree_worstInputCost}
\leanok
\uses{FABL.RandomizedDecisionTree.inputCost, FABL.majorityThreeRandomizedTree, FABL.majorityThreeRandomizedTree_inputCost, FABL.majorityThreeWorstInput}
\difficulty{3}
On the input $(1,1,-1)$, the randomized decision tree's expected number of queries is
$8/3$.
\end{theorem}

\begin{theorem}[Worst-Case Expected Query Cost Bound]
\lean{FABL.majorityThreeRandomizedTree_worstCaseCost_le}
\label{FABL.majorityThreeRandomizedTree_worstCaseCost_le}
\leanok
\uses{FABL.RandomizedDecisionTree.worstCaseCost, FABL.majorityThreeRandomizedTree, FABL.majorityThreeRandomizedTree_inputCost_le}
\difficulty{3}
The maximum, over all three-coordinate sign inputs, of the randomized decision tree's
expected number of queries is at most $8/3$.
\end{theorem}

  {pdf-ffbe9c7b3306-p231-b003}
For three independent uniformly distributed signs in $\{-1,1\}$, the decision tree that
queries the first two signs and queries the third exactly when the first two disagree
has expected query count $5/2$.
\end{theorem}

  {FABL.recursiveMajorityRandomizedCostBound_zero}

\proofstep
  {FABL.recursiveMajorityAverageCostBound_zero}
  {context}
  {Analysis-of-Boolean-Functions-by-Ryan-ODonnell}
  {pdf-ffbe9c7b3306-p230-b004,
    pdf-ffbe9c7b3306-p231-b003}
For inputs in $\{-1,1\}^3$, let majority return $1$ when the sum of the three
coordinates is nonnegative and $-1$ otherwise. The randomized decision-tree complexity
of this function, measured by the infimum of the worst-case expected number of queried
coordinates among finite-seed, zero-error randomized decision trees, is at most $8/3$.
\end{theorem}

\begin{definition}[Deterministic randomized tree for three-bit majority]
\lean{FABL.majorityThreeDeterministicRandomizedTree}
\label{FABL.majorityThreeDeterministicRandomizedTree}
\leanok
\uses{FABL.RandomizedDecisionTree, FABL.RandomizedDecisionTree.ofDeterministic, FABL.Sign, FABL.majority, FABL.majorityThreeTree01, FABL.majorityThreeTree01_computes}
There is a randomized decision tree on three signs whose seed space is finite and
nonempty, and every seed selects a deterministic decision tree that computes majority on
three inputs with zero error.
\end{definition}

  {pdf-ffbe9c7b3306-p231-b003}
For the specified randomized decision tree computing majority on three signs, when the
three input signs are independently uniform in $\{-1,1\}$, the expected number of
queried coordinates, also averaged over the tree's seed distribution, is $5/2$.
\end{theorem}

\begin{theorem}[Majority on three signs]
\lean{FABL.averageDecisionTreeComplexity_majority_three_le}
\proofsource{Analysis-of-Boolean-Functions-by-Ryan-ODonnell}{pdf-ffbe9c7b3306-p230-b004}
\label{FABL.averageDecisionTreeComplexity_majority_three_le}
\leanok
\uses{FABL.RandomizedDecisionTree.averageComplexity, FABL.RandomizedDecisionTree.averageCost_nonneg, FABL.Sign, FABL.majority, FABL.majorityThreeDeterministicRandomizedTree, FABL.majorityThreeDeterministicRandomizedTree_averageCost, FABL.uniformPMF}
\difficulty{4}
Under the uniform distribution on the three-dimensional sign cube, the minimum average
query cost of a zero-error randomized decision tree computing majority is at most $5/2$.
\end{theorem}

\begin{definition}[Finite geometric sum for query cost]
\lean{FABL.orAverageQueryCost}
\statementsource{Analysis-of-Boolean-Functions-by-Ryan-ODonnell}{pdf-ffbe9c7b3306-p231-b004}
\label{FABL.orAverageQueryCost}
\leanok
For a natural number $n$ and a real number $p$, define the average query-cost expression
by $\sum_{k=0}^{n-1}(1-p)^k$.
\end{definition}

  {pdf-ffbe9c7b3306-p231-b003}
Let $n$ be a nonnegative integer and let $p\in\mathbb{R}$ be nonzero. Then
$\sum_{k=0}^{n-1}(1-p)^k=\frac{1-(1-p)^n}{p}$.
\end{theorem}

\begin{theorem}[Recurrence for average query cost]
\lean{FABL.orAverageQueryCost_succ}
\label{FABL.orAverageQueryCost_succ}
\leanok
\uses{FABL.orAverageQueryCost}
\difficulty{3}
For every natural number $n$ and real number $p$, the average query cost at $n+1$
satisfies $C_{n+1}(p)=1+(1-p)C_n(p)$, where $C_n(p)=\\sum_{k=0}^{n-1}(1-p)^k$.
\end{theorem}

\begin{theorem}[Average query cost at the critical parameter]
\lean{FABL.orAverageQueryCost_at_critical}
\label{FABL.orAverageQueryCost_at_critical}
\leanok
\uses{FABL.orAverageQueryCost, FABL.orAverageQueryCost_eq}
\difficulty{3}
Let $n$ be a nonnegative integer and let $p\in\mathbb{R}$ be nonzero. If
$(1-p)^n=\frac12$, then $\sum_{k=0}^{n-1}(1-p)^k=\frac{1}{2p}$.
\end{theorem}

\begin{definition}[Recursive majority cost bound]
\lean{FABL.recursiveMajorityRandomizedCostBound}
\statementsource{Analysis-of-Boolean-Functions-by-Ryan-ODonnell}{pdf-ffbe9c7b3306-p231-b003}
\label{FABL.recursiveMajorityRandomizedCostBound}
\leanok
For a natural number $d$, define the recursive majority randomized cost bound to be
$(8/3)^d$.
\end{definition}

\begin{definition}[Recursive majority cost bound]
\lean{FABL.recursiveMajorityAverageCostBound}
\statementsource{Analysis-of-Boolean-Functions-by-Ryan-ODonnell}{pdf-ffbe9c7b3306-p231-b003}
\label{FABL.recursiveMajorityAverageCostBound}
\leanok
For each natural number $d$, define the recursive majority average cost bound to be
$(5/2)^d$.
\end{definition}

\begin{theorem}[Initial randomized cost bound]
\lean{FABL.recursiveMajorityRandomizedCostBound_zero}
\label{FABL.recursiveMajorityRandomizedCostBound_zero}
\leanok
\uses{FABL.recursiveMajorityRandomizedCostBound}
\difficulty{1}
The randomized cost bound at depth $0$ is $1$.
\end{theorem}

\begin{theorem}[Randomized cost bound recurrence]
\lean{FABL.recursiveMajorityRandomizedCostBound_succ}
\label{FABL.recursiveMajorityRandomizedCostBound_succ}
\leanok
\uses{FABL.recursiveMajorityRandomizedCostBound}
\difficulty{1}
For every natural number $d$, the randomized cost bound at depth $d+1$ equals
$\frac{8}{3}$ times the randomized cost bound at depth $d$.
\end{theorem}

\begin{theorem}[Initial recursive majority cost bound]
\lean{FABL.recursiveMajorityAverageCostBound_zero}
\label{FABL.recursiveMajorityAverageCostBound_zero}
\leanok
\uses{FABL.recursiveMajorityAverageCostBound}
\difficulty{1}
For the recursively defined average cost bound $B(d)=(5/2)^d$ at each nonnegative
integer depth $d$, the value at depth $0$ is $B(0)=1$.
\end{theorem}

\begin{theorem}[Average cost bound recurrence]
\lean{FABL.recursiveMajorityAverageCostBound_succ}
\label{FABL.recursiveMajorityAverageCostBound_succ}
\leanok
\uses{FABL.recursiveMajorityAverageCostBound}
\difficulty{1}
For every natural number $d$, the average cost bound at depth $d+1$ equals $\frac{5}{2}$
times the average cost bound at depth $d$.
\end{theorem}
